base.summary: The box, and only the box — Field owns the label, helper text, message and disabled dimming. Every value below is the one `.rata-text-field-input` uses, deliberately: the two controls sit in the same form and a reader should not be able to tell they were built separately.

tokens.font-family: font.family.sans — a control inherits neither family nor size from the page, so both are stated
tokens.font-size: type.control.size.md — the same constant the button family and the text field use, so all three measure their text alike
tokens.line-height: type.control.line-height.md — and here it also decides the height, since `rows` multiplies it
tokens.padding-inline: space.control.padding-inline.md — matching the text field's md step, which is the only step this control has
tokens.padding-block: space.padding.xs — a single-line control centres its text with its height, and a multi-line one has no height to centre against, so the space has to be stated

states.summary: Selected from the primitive's data-status on the Field root, exactly as the text field's are. The rings are inset strokes, never the focus ring, so a control can be focused and invalid at once.

tokens.hover inner band: theme.bg.muted at border.2 as an inset shadow, idle only — the validation rings occupy the same 2px and box-shadow does not accumulate
tokens.focus outline: focus.ring-width solid theme.fg.primary at space.0 offset — the same deliberate departure the text field documents, so the two controls' focus looks identical
tokens.disabled cursor: not-allowed — the dimming itself is Field's, on the root

behavior.summary: A `<textarea>` inside a `Field`. No primitive of its own: `getFieldProps` already supplies every id and ARIA attribute, and a multi-line control needs nothing a single-line one does not.

decisions.decision: A separate component, not a `multiline` prop on TextField
decisions.why: `TextField` is typed to `HTMLInputElement` and forwards its ref as one, so a boolean that silently swapped the element would invalidate half its props at runtime while still compiling. The elements also differ in ways a caller has to know about: `rows` and `wrap` exist on one and not the other, and Enter inserts a newline here where it submits there. This system's test for splitting is a difference in semantics rather than in looks, and that is what this is — the same test that separated Text from Heading.

decisions.decision: `rows` sets the height, and there is no `size` prop
decisions.why: `TextField`'s `size` exists to choose a control height from the control scale. A multi-line control's height is how many lines it shows, which is what `rows` already says — offering both would be two props for one measurement, and a caller would have to guess which wins.

decisions.decision: It does not grow with its content in this version
decisions.why: The honest options are all costly: `field-sizing: content` is not supported widely enough to be the only mechanism, the replicated-content grid trick needs a wrapper element around the control that exists purely to be measured, and measuring in JS means a resize observer per field. Each is a real decision about the DOM this component puts on the page, and none of them should ride along with the box. `rows` plus a resize handle covers the case meanwhile, and the caller can see how much room they are giving.

decisions.decision: `resize` defaults to `vertical`, and horizontal is not offered
decisions.why: Letting a reader make the box taller is the cheapest possible fix for a field that turned out too small, and it costs the layout nothing — the control's inline size is the form's. Horizontal resize does cost the layout: a control dragged wider than its column overflows whatever contains it, and no form anticipates that. `none` is there for the layouts that cannot tolerate a height change either.

A counter is two things — a number that updates, and an announcement policy for when it should interrupt a typist — and both belong to the caller who knows the limit. `Field` already has the slot: `description` for the limit stated up front, `message` with `status="invalid"` for having passed it. Building it in would mean choosing a live-region policy on everyone's behalf.
Nothing new is decided here; it is named so the contract does not read as though the question were open. The same consequence applies — a readOnly control still submits its value.

label.summary: The control's label. Always required — `labelHidden` hides it, nothing removes it.
use: A short noun phrase naming what goes in it: "Release notes", not "Type your release notes".
dont: Leaving it off because a placeholder says the same thing. The placeholder is gone on the first keystroke.
label.a11y: Bound to the control by Field, so it is the accessible name and clicking it focuses the control.

rows.summary: How many lines of text the control shows before it scrolls.
use: Three for a note, eight or more for something someone will draft in.
A number that matches what you expect, so the reader can see how much is wanted of them.
dont: One. A single-line control is a `TextField`, and a one-row textarea is that with worse keyboard behaviour — Enter inserts a newline instead of submitting.

resize.summary: Whether the reader may drag the control taller.
use: `none` only where a taller control would break the layout around it — a fixed-height panel, a row in a dense table.
dont: `none` as a default because the handle looks untidy. It is the cheapest fix a reader has for a field that turned out too small, and taking it away costs them more than it saves you.

labelHidden.summary: Takes the label off screen while leaving it in the accessibility tree.
use: A control whose meaning is already carried by a heading directly above it.
dont: Pairing it with a placeholder standing in for the name.
labelHidden.a11y: The label element is still rendered and still bound. Only the pixels go.

id.summary: Stable id for the control, when something outside needs to point at it.
use: A form library that addresses fields by id, or an error summary linking to the control it names.
dont: Reusing one across two fields. Every id under it is derived from this.

status.summary: Validation lifecycle, driving the message tone, `aria-invalid`, `aria-busy` and the ring.
use: `invalid` with a `message` saying what to do about it.
dont: `invalid` with no message. The ring says something is wrong; only the message says what.
status.a11y: Field's, unchanged: `invalid` sets `aria-invalid` and pulls the message into `aria-describedby`, and while idle the message stays on the page but leaves the chain.

description.summary: Persistent helper text under the control.
use: The length limit, stated before someone writes past it — this is where a counter's job mostly lives.
dont: Repeating the label in a sentence. It is read out after the name.
description.a11y: Joins `aria-describedby` ahead of the message, so a constraint is heard before a failure.

use: What to do about an `invalid` status, in the imperative: "Keep this under 500 characters."
dont: Putting the permanent limit here. It leaves the description chain whenever the status returns to idle — that is `description`.
message.a11y: Announced politely rather than as an alert, because it is already in `aria-describedby`.

required.summary: Marks the control required, in the label and to assistive technology.
dont: Pairing it with a hand-written asterisk in `label`. Field renders one.
required.a11y: `aria-required` on the control; the rendered marker is `aria-hidden`.

disabled.summary: Blocks editing while keeping the control focusable, readable and announced.
use: A note whose content is decided elsewhere and should still be readable in full.
dont: Assuming the value is withheld. `readOnly` still submits.
disabled.a11y: `aria-disabled` plus `readOnly` from Field, never the native attribute.

className.summary: Class for the wrapper — the width the form wants, not a restyle.
use: The measure or grid placement the form decides.
dont: Setting a height. That is `rows`, and a hand-written height stops matching the line count the reader sees.

usage.case: A note someone will actually draft in
usage.when: The commonest case: free text with a stated limit.
usage.example:
<Textarea
  label="Release notes"
  rows={8}
  description="Markdown is fine. Around 500 characters reads best."
/>
usage.notes: The limit goes in `description` rather than a counter, because it is the thing worth knowing BEFORE writing. Eight rows says how much is wanted more honestly than any sentence would.

usage.when: Reporting a limit the writer has passed.
usage.example:
<Textarea
  label="Release notes"
  status="invalid"
  message="Keep this under 500 characters."
/>
usage.notes: The message is the imperative, not the diagnosis — "too long" tells someone what happened, this tells them what to do. The ring and the colour say it twice more.

usage.case: A layout that cannot take a taller control
usage.when: A fixed-height panel, or a control inside a dense row.
usage.notes: `none` because the container genuinely cannot grow, which is the only reason for it. The label is hidden rather than absent — the row's own header is carrying the name visually, and nothing about the accessible name changes.

usage.when: The value is one line and Enter should submit the form.
usage.notes: Don't. That is `TextField`. A one-row textarea looks almost right and behaves wrong: Enter inserts a newline instead of submitting, and the value can arrive with line breaks in it that nothing upstream expects.
